questions.sub: Classification and Normal Counts of Leukocytes
questions.q: What is the normal total leukocyte (white blood cell) count in peripheral venous blood of a healthy adult?
questions.explain: Normal adult total WBC count ranges from 4,000 to 11,000/uL (4.0 to 11.0 x 10^9/L). Counts below 4,000/uL indicate leukopenia, whereas counts above 11,000/uL indicate leukocytosis.

open.q: State the normal reference range for total white blood cell (leukocyte) count in a healthy adult.

questions.sub: Classification and Normal Counts of Leukocytes
questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks the five types of circulating leukocytes in healthy adults from most abundant to least abundant?
questions.explain: In healthy adults, neutrophils make up 50-70%, lymphocytes 20-40%, monocytes 2-8%, eosinophils 1-4%, and basophils less than 1% (0.5-1%) of total circulating leukocytes.

open.q: List the five types of peripheral blood leukocytes in descending order of their normal percentage in healthy adults.

questions.sub: Classification and Normal Counts of Leukocytes
questions.q: Which leukocytes are classified as agranulocytes because they lack specific secondary cytoplasmic granules?
questions.explain: Lymphocytes and monocytes have round or kidney-shaped nuclei and lack specific secondary granules (though they contain nonspecific azurophilic lysosomes), whereas neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils are polymorphonuclear granulocytes.

open.q: Name the two classes of human leukocytes classified as agranulocytes.

questions.q: Which colony-stimulating factor specifically promotes the terminal differentiation and functional activation of neutrophils from granulocyte-monocyte progenitors?
questions.explain: G-CSF drives neutrophil lineage commitment, maturation, release from bone marrow, and phagocytic activity; IL-5 stimulates eosinophils, while EPO and TPO regulate red cells and platelets respectively.

open.q: Name the hematopoietic cytokine that specifically stimulates the production, maturation, and bone marrow release of neutrophils.

questions.q: What is the approximate half-life of a mature neutrophil in the bloodstream once released from the bone marrow?
questions.explain: Mature neutrophils circulate in blood for only 6 to 8 hours (total blood transit under 24 hours) before migrating into tissues where they survive another 1 to 4 days; the bone marrow stores a 5-day reserve pool.

open.q: What is the normal intravascular half-life of a mature circulating neutrophil?

questions.q: Which primary (azurophilic) granule enzyme in neutrophils catalyzes the reaction of hydrogen peroxide with chloride ions to produce bactericidal hypochlorous acid (HOCl)?
questions.explain: During the respiratory burst, NADPH oxidase generates superoxide, superoxide dismutase forms H2O2, and myeloperoxidase (MPO) combines H2O2 with Cl- to generate potent hypochlorous acid (bleach).

open.q: Name the azurophilic granule enzyme in neutrophils that converts hydrogen peroxide and chloride ions into hypochlorous acid during the respiratory burst.

questions.q: Which step of leukocyte extravasation into inflamed tissue involves low-affinity rolling along vascular endothelial cells mediated by selectins binding sialyl-Lewis X carbohydrates?
options: Firm integrin-mediated arrest via LFA-1 and ICAM-1
questions.explain: Endothelial E-selectin and P-selectin bind sialyl-Lewis X on neutrophils to slow them down (rolling), followed by chemokine-activated integrin (LFA-1/Mac-1) binding to ICAM-1 for firm adhesion, and PECAM-1 (CD31) for diapedesis.

open.q: Which adhesion molecules mediate the initial rolling step of neutrophils along inflamed postcapillary venule endothelium?

questions.q: Which pair of molecules acts as the two most potent physiological opsonins that coat bacteria to enhance phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages?
questions.explain: Phagocytes express surface Fc-gamma receptors for IgG and complement receptors (CR1) for C3b, dramatically accelerating attachment and engulfment of encapsulated microbes.

open.q: Name the two major serum opsonins that coat microbes to facilitate phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages.

questions.q: Which complement cleavage product serves as a powerful chemotactic attractant recruiting neutrophils to sites of bacterial infection?
questions.explain: C5a, along with leukotriene B4 (LTB4), interleukin-8 (CXCL8), kallikrein, and bacterial N-formylmethionyl peptides, forms a chemical gradient guiding directional neutrophil chemotaxis.

open.q: Name the complement fragment that acts as a major chemoattractant for neutrophils during acute inflammation.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy suffers recurrent life-threatening abscesses caused by catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus. His neutrophils phagocytose bacteria normally but fail to generate reactive oxygen species (negative nitroblue tetrazolium test). Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is caused by defective phagocyte NADPH oxidase; patients handle catalase-negative bacteria (which make their own H2O2) but cannot kill catalase-positive microbes that degrade their own H2O2.

open.q: In chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), deficiency of which phagocyte enzyme prevents the oxidative respiratory burst?

questions.q: A newborn presents with delayed umbilical cord separation at 4 weeks, marked neutrophilia (45,000/mm3), and recurrent non-purulent skin infections lacking pus formation. Flow cytometry shows absent CD18 (beta-2 integrin) on leukocytes. What process is impaired?
options: Firm endothelial adhesion and extravasation of neutrophils into tissues
questions.explain: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (LAD-1) results from defective CD18 beta-2 integrin subunits (LFA-1, Mac-1), trapping neutrophils inside blood vessels so they cannot migrate into tissues to form pus.

open.q: In leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (defective CD18 integrin), why are infected wounds devoid of pus despite severe peripheral neutrophilia?
accept: Neutrophils cannot firmly adhere to endothelium or migrate into tissues
Impaired neutrophil extravasation and firm adhesion

questions.q: What are the two principal physiological roles of eosinophils?
options: Phagocytosing encapsulated pneumococci and secreting antibodies
Synthesizing coagulation factors and clearing senescent red cells
Presenting antigens to naive T cells and producing interferon-alpha
Destroying multicellular helminth parasites via major basic protein and modulating allergic inflammation
questions.explain: Eosinophils attach to IgE-coated helminths and release cationic granules (major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein, eosinophil peroxidase) while also releasing histaminase and arylsulfatase to dampen mast cell mediators in allergy.

open.q: State the two primary immune functions of eosinophils.
accept: Defense against helminth parasites and modulation of allergic reactions
Killing parasitic worms and regulating type I hypersensitivity

questions.q: Which cytokine secreted predominantly by Th2 lymphocytes specifically stimulates eosinophil production, activation, and survival?
questions.explain: IL-5 is the signature eosinophilopoietic cytokine produced by Th2 cells and type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2), explaining eosinophilia in helminthiasis and allergic asthma.

open.q: Name the Th2 cytokine that specifically stimulates eosinophil differentiation and activation.

questions.q: Which preformed vasoactive and anticoagulant mediators are stored within the metachromatic basophilic granules of basophils and tissue mast cells?
questions.explain: Basophils and mast cells express high-affinity Fc-epsilon-RI receptors for IgE and release preformed histamine (vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability) and heparin (local anticoagulant) upon allergen cross-linking.

open.q: Name two major preformed mediators stored in the cytoplasmic granules of basophils and mast cells.

questions.q: How is degranulation of sensitized tissue mast cells triggered during an immediate type I hypersensitivity reaction?
options: Binding of monomeric IgG to complement C1q
Cross-linking of two adjacent surface-bound IgE molecules by a multivalent antigen
Activation of Fas death receptors by cytotoxic T cells
questions.explain: Monomeric IgE bound to Fc-epsilon-RI does not activate mast cells alone; bridging of at least two IgE-Fc-epsilon-RI complexes by multivalent allergen triggers tyrosine kinase signaling, Ca2+ influx, and exocytosis of granules.

open.q: What molecular event on the surface of a sensitized mast cell triggers rapid degranulation during an allergic reaction?
accept: Cross-linking of surface-bound IgE antibodies by allergen
Bridging of two adjacent IgE molecules on Fc-epsilon-RI receptors by antigen

questions.q: After circulating in blood for about 24 to 72 hours, monocytes migrate into tissues and differentiate into specialized tissue macrophages. Which tissue-resident macrophage is correctly matched with its organ?
options: Kupffer cells in the central nervous system
questions.explain: Members of the mononuclear phagocyte system include Kupffer cells (liver), microglia (CNS), alveolar macrophages/dust cells (lungs), Langerhans cells (epidermis), and multinucleated osteoclasts (bone).

open.q: Name the tissue-resident macrophages located in the hepatic sinusoids and in the central nervous system.

questions.q: Which three cell types serve as the professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) capable of expressing MHC class II and activating naive CD4+ T helper cells?
options: Dendritic cells, macrophages, and B lymphocytes
Natural killer cells, CD8+ T cells, and platelets
questions.explain: Dendritic cells (most potent for naive T cells), macrophages, and B cells constitutively or inducibly express MHC class II and costimulatory B7 (CD80/CD86) molecules to prime CD4+ T cells.

open.q: Name the three types of professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) in the human immune system.
accept: Dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells

questions.q: Which characteristic distinguishes innate immunity from adaptive (acquired) immunity?
options: Innate immunity requires several days of clonal expansion before acting
Innate immunity acts rapidly through germline-encoded pattern-recognition receptors and lacks antigen-specific memory
Innate immunity depends on somatic V(D)J recombination
Innate immunity is mediated exclusively by plasma cells and cytotoxic T cells
questions.explain: Innate immunity provides immediate, non-specific defense via barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, and complement recognizing conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), without antigen-specific memory.

open.q: State two key differences between innate immunity and adaptive immunity regarding response speed and immunological memory.
accept: Innate immunity acts immediately without memory, whereas adaptive immunity has a lag phase and develops specific memory
Innate is immediate and lacks memory; adaptive is delayed and has memory

questions.q: Which innate immune receptors on macrophages and dendritic cells recognize conserved microbial structures such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS), flagellin, and double-stranded viral RNA?
questions.explain: Toll-like receptors (such as TLR4 for Gram-negative LPS, TLR3 for viral dsRNA, and TLR5 for flagellin) are germline-encoded pattern recognition receptors that activate NF-kappa-B to induce proinflammatory cytokines.

open.q: Name the family of pattern recognition receptors on innate immune cells that detects conserved microbial molecules such as bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS).

questions.q: How do Natural Killer (NK) cells recognize and destroy virus-infected cells or tumor cells without prior antigen sensitization?
options: By recognising viral peptides presented on MHC class II
By secreting high-affinity neutralising IgG antibodies
By phagocytosing whole tumour cells intact
By detecting reduced MHC I expression and other stress signals on target cells
questions.explain: NK cells possess inhibitory receptors (KIRs) that recognize normal self MHC class I; when viruses or tumors downregulate MHC class I to evade CD8+ T cells, inhibition is lost and NK cells release perforin and granzymes to induce apoptosis.

open.q: Explain the 'missing-self' mechanism by which Natural Killer (NK) cells identify virus-infected or malignant cells.
accept: Loss or downregulation of self MHC class I removes inhibitory signals on NK cells
Decreased surface MHC class I fails to engage NK inhibitory receptors, triggering killing

questions.q: Which cytokines are secreted by virus-infected cells to induce an antiviral state in neighboring uninfected cells by degrading viral mRNA and inhibiting viral protein translation?
questions.explain: IFN-alpha (leukocytes) and IFN-beta (fibroblasts) bind neighboring cell receptors to activate RNase L (degrades viral RNA) and protein kinase R (inhibits eIF2 translation initiation), while also enhancing NK cell activity.

open.q: Name the two Type I interferons released by virus-infected cells to protect neighboring cells against viral replication.

questions.q: Which complement activation pathway is initiated directly by antigen-antibody complexes containing IgM or IgG?
questions.explain: C1q binds the Fc portion of IgM (single pentamer) or paired IgG molecules bound to antigen, activating C1r and C1s to cleave C4 and C2 into the classical C3 convertase (C4b2a).

open.q: Which pathway of complement activation is triggered when C1q binds to IgM or IgG immune complexes?

questions.q: On which central complement protein do the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways all converge?
questions.explain: All three pathways generate a C3 convertase (C4b2a or C3bBb) that cleaves C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin and subunit of C5 convertase).

open.q: Name the central complement protein where the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways converge.

questions.q: Which complement components assemble to form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC) that punches transmembrane pores in target pathogens such as Neisseria species?
options: Factor B, Factor D, and properdin
C5b, C6, C7, C8, and polymerized C9
questions.explain: C5b sequentially binds C6, C7, C8, and multiple C9 monomers (C5b-9) to insert a lytic pore into Gram-negative outer membranes; deficiency of terminal MAC proteins predisposes strongly to recurrent Neisseria infections.

open.q: List the complement proteins that form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC).

questions.q: Which complement fragments act as anaphylatoxins that trigger mast cell degranulation, histamine release, smooth muscle contraction, and increased vascular permeability?
questions.explain: C3a and especially C5a bind anaphylatoxin receptors on mast cells, basophils, and vascular smooth muscle to induce acute inflammatory vascular responses.

open.q: Name the two most potent complement anaphylatoxins that induce mast cell degranulation and increased vascular permeability.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of painless, non-pruritic swelling of her lips, eyelids, and larynx precipitated by minor dental trauma. Serum C4 is markedly decreased and C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) activity is low. Which vasoactive mediator directly causes her edema?
questions.explain: Hereditary angioedema is caused by C1-INH deficiency; besides inhibiting C1r/C1s, C1-INH normally inhibits kallikrein, so its absence leads to unopposed bradykinin generation and severe vascular permeability (unresponsive to antihistamines).

open.q: In hereditary angioedema caused by C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, overproduction of which vasoactive peptide causes non-pitting mucosal and laryngeal edema?

questions.q: Where do B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes undergo antigen-independent maturation and selection, respectively?
options: B cells in the spleen; T cells in the lymph nodes
B cells in the thymus; T cells in the bone marrow
B cells in the bone marrow; T cells in the thymus
Both B and T cells mature exclusively in Peyer's patches
questions.explain: Both originate from bone marrow lymphoid progenitors, but B cells complete maturation in the bone marrow whereas pro-T cells migrate to the thymus to undergo positive and negative selection.

open.q: Name the primary lymphoid organs in which B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes mature in humans.
accept: Bone marrow for B cells and thymus for T cells
B cells: bone marrow; T cells: thymus

questions.q: During T-cell maturation in the thymus, what is the purpose of positive selection in the thymic cortex versus negative selection in the thymic medulla?
options: Positive selection deletes autoreactive T cells; negative selection tests TCR affinity for foreign antigens
Positive selection induces class switching; negative selection induces somatic hypermutation
Positive selection converts CD4+ cells into B cells; negative selection triggers apoptosis of macrophages
Positive selection retains T cells able to recognize self MHC molecules; negative selection deletes T cells that bind self-peptides too strongly
questions.explain: Positive selection ensures MHC restriction (survival of thymocytes whose TCRs weakly bind self-MHC on cortical epithelial cells), while negative selection enforces central self-tolerance by eliminating high-affinity self-reactive clones via AIRE-expressed tissue antigens.

open.q: Contrast the roles of positive selection and negative selection during T-cell development in the thymus.
accept: Positive selection selects for self-MHC recognition; negative selection eliminates strongly self-reactive T cells
Positive selection ensures MHC restriction, negative selection establishes central tolerance

questions.q: Which class of Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) molecules presents endogenous intracellular peptides (such as viral proteins) to CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes?
questions.explain: MHC class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) is expressed on all nucleated cells and platelets, displays cytosolic peptides loaded via TAP in the ER, and interacts with the CD8 coreceptor (rule of 8: 1 x 8 = 8).

open.q: Which MHC class is expressed on all nucleated cells and presents endogenous peptides to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells?

questions.q: Which class of MHC molecules presents exogenous phagocytosed peptides to CD4+ helper T lymphocytes?
questions.explain: MHC class II (HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, HLA-DR) is restricted to professional APCs, presents degraded endosomal/lysosomal peptides after invariant chain cleavage, and binds the CD4 coreceptor (rule of 8: 2 x 4 = 8).

open.q: Which MHC class is expressed on professional antigen-presenting cells and presents exogenous peptides to CD4+ helper T cells?

questions.q: Full activation of a naive T lymphocyte requires two signals from an antigen-presenting cell. What constitutes Signal 1 and Signal 2?
options: Signal 1 is IL-2 binding; Signal 2 is complement C3b binding
Signal 1 is CD40-CD40L interaction; Signal 2 is histamine release
Signal 1 is TCR binding peptide-MHC; Signal 2 is costimulatory B7 (CD80/CD86) binding CD28 on the T cell
Signal 1 is IgE cross-linking; Signal 2 is perforin secretion
questions.explain: TCR recognition of peptide-MHC (Signal 1) without B7-CD28 costimulation (Signal 2) drives the T cell into clonal anergy (unresponsiveness) rather than proliferation.

open.q: Identify the receptor-ligand pairs responsible for Signal 1 and Signal 2 during naive T-cell activation.
accept: Signal 1: TCR with peptide-MHC; Signal 2: CD28 with B7 (CD80/CD86)

questions.q: Which cytokine acts as the primary autocrine and paracrine growth factor driving clonal proliferation of activated T lymphocytes?
questions.explain: Activated T cells synthesize IL-2 and upregulate the high-affinity alpha-chain (CD25) of the IL-2 receptor, stimulating rapid clonal expansion of effector and memory T cells.

open.q: Name the key cytokine that stimulates clonal proliferation of activated T cells.

questions.q: Which CD4+ T helper subset secretes interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) to activate macrophages for intracellular killing of mycobacteria and other intracellular pathogens?
questions.explain: Differentiation of Th1 cells is driven by APC-derived IL-12; Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma to enhance macrophage phagolysosomal fusion and nitric oxide/ROS killing of intracellular organisms like Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

open.q: Which CD4+ T helper cell subset secretes IFN-gamma to activate macrophages against intracellular bacteria such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis?

questions.q: Which CD4+ T helper subset secretes IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 to promote IgE class switching, eosinophil recruitment, and mucosal defense against helminths?
questions.explain: Th2 cells coordinate humoral/allergic and anti-helminth immunity via IL-4 (IgE class switching), IL-5 (eosinophil activation), and IL-13 (mucus secretion and airway hyperreactivity).

open.q: Name the CD4+ T helper subset that produces IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 to drive IgE production and anti-helminth immunity.

questions.q: Which T-cell subset expresses FOXP3 and CD25 and suppresses excessive immune responses to maintain peripheral self-tolerance via IL-10 and TGF-beta?
questions.explain: FOXP3+ CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T cells secrete anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10 and TGF-beta) and express CTLA-4 to restrain autoreactive lymphocytes; FOXP3 loss causes IPEX syndrome.

open.q: Name the immunosuppressive T-cell population characterized by the transcription factor FOXP3 and cytokines IL-10 and TGF-beta.

questions.q: By which two main mechanisms do activated CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) induce apoptosis in virus-infected target cells?
options: Complement C1q activation and histamine release
Neutralizing IgA secretion and bradykinin synthesis
Exocytosis of perforin and granzymes, and engagement of target Fas (CD95) by Fas ligand (FasL)
questions.explain: Perforin forms pores in the target membrane allowing granzymes to enter and cleave intracellular caspases, while FasL-Fas binding activates the extrinsic caspase-8 apoptotic cascade.

open.q: State the two mechanisms by which CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes trigger apoptosis in target cells.
accept: Perforin and granzymes, and Fas ligand binding to Fas

questions.q: Which cells terminally differentiate from activated B lymphocytes to secrete large quantities of specific antibodies?
questions.explain: Upon antigen stimulation and T-cell help, B cells proliferate in germinal centers and differentiate into memory B cells or antibody-secreting plasma cells with abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and eccentric clock-face nuclei.

open.q: Name the terminally differentiated B-lineage cells responsible for high-rate antibody secretion.

questions.q: Which molecular interaction between a B lymphocyte and a CD4+ T helper cell is essential for immunoglobulin class-switch recombination and germinal center formation?
options: B-cell CD40 binding CD40 ligand (CD40L / CD154) on activated Th cells
B-cell MHC class I binding CD8
questions.explain: CD40-CD40L engagement alongside T-cell cytokines activates activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) in B cells to drive isotype switching (IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE) and somatic hypermutation; CD40L deficiency causes Hyper-IgM syndrome.

open.q: Which costimulatory receptor-ligand interaction between B cells and CD4+ T helper cells is required for antibody class switching?

questions.q: What is the basic structural composition of a single monomeric immunoglobulin molecule?
options: One heavy chain and three light chains linked by peptide bonds
Four identical alpha-globin chains surrounding a heme ring
Two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains (kappa or lambda) joined by disulfide bonds
Three heavy chains and one J chain without disulfide bridges
questions.explain: Every immunoglobulin monomer consists of 2 identical heavy chains (determining class: gamma, mu, alpha, delta, or epsilon) and 2 identical light chains (kappa or lambda), forming two antigen-binding Fab regions and one effector Fc region.

open.q: Describe the polypeptide chain composition of a monomeric antibody molecule.
accept: Two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bonds

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin isotype is the most abundant in human serum (~75-80%) and is the only antibody class capable of crossing the placenta to confer passive immunity to the fetus?
questions.explain: IgG is transported across syncytiotrophoblasts via the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), protecting newborns during the first months of life; it also fixes complement and acts as a major opsonin.

open.q: Which immunoglobulin class crosses the human placenta to provide passive immunity to the newborn?

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin is secreted predominantly as a J-chain-linked pentamer, is the first antibody produced in a primary immune response, and is the most efficient activator of the classical complement pathway?
questions.explain: Pentameric IgM has 10 antigen-binding sites (high avidity) and multiple closely spaced Fc regions that readily bind C1q; because it cannot cross the placenta, elevated IgM in cord blood indicates congenital intrauterine infection.

open.q: Which immunoglobulin isotype exists as a pentamer in serum, predominates early in a primary immune response, and fixes complement most potently?

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin isotype predominates in mucosal secretions (saliva, tears, breast milk, respiratory and intestinal mucus) as a dimer stabilized by a J chain and secretory component?
questions.explain: Secretory IgA (sIgA) acquires its secretory component during transcytosis across mucosal epithelial cells, protecting it from luminal proteases while neutralizing microbes at mucosal surfaces.

open.q: Name the predominant dimeric immunoglobulin found in breast milk, saliva, tears, and gastrointestinal secretions.

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin has the lowest serum concentration, binds high-affinity Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils, and mediates immediate hypersensitivity and defense against helminths?
questions.explain: IgE circulates at nanogram levels because most of it is bound tightly to Fc-epsilon-RI on tissue mast cells and basophils, sensitizing them for rapid degranulation upon allergen or parasite encounter.

open.q: Which immunoglobulin mediates type I allergic reactions and anti-helminth immunity by binding to mast cells and basophils?

questions.q: How does a secondary (anamnestic) humoral immune response differ from a primary immune response upon re-exposure to the same protein antigen?
options: Longer lag phase, lower peak titre and predominantly IgM
Absence of memory B cells and no affinity maturation
Exclusive production of IgD without class switching
Shorter lag phase, higher titre and predominantly high-affinity class-switched antibodies
questions.explain: Pre-existing long-lived memory B and T cells that already underwent somatic hypermutation and class switching respond within 1 to 3 days (versus 7 to 10 days in primary exposure) with robust high-affinity IgG.

open.q: State three ways in which a secondary immune response differs from a primary immune response.
accept: Shorter lag phase, higher antibody titer, and predominantly high-affinity IgG
Faster onset, greater magnitude, and class-switched IgG predominance

questions.sub: Active vs Passive Immunity and Hypersensitivity
questions.q: Administration of tetanus immunoglobulin (human anti-tetanus antibodies) or maternal transplacental transfer of IgG provides which type of immunity?
questions.explain: Passive immunity transfers preformed antibodies from an external source, conferring immediate but temporary protection (weeks to a few months) without stimulating host memory B or T cells.

open.q: What type of immunity is conferred by receiving preformed antibodies such as maternal IgG across the placenta or antivenom serum?

questions.sub: Active vs Passive Immunity and Hypersensitivity
questions.q: Which Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by T lymphocytes rather than antibodies, taking 48 to 72 hours to peak (as seen in the tuberculin/Mantoux skin test and poison ivy contact dermatitis)?
questions.explain: Type IV hypersensitivity is antibody-independent; sensitized Th1 cells release IFN-gamma and TNF to recruit and activate macrophages (induration at 48-72 h), or CD8+ CTLs directly lyse target cells.

open.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by T lymphocytes and macrophages rather than antibodies, exemplified by the Mantoux tuberculin skin test?

questions.sub: Active vs Passive Immunity and Hypersensitivity
questions.q: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome, and acute hemolytic transfusion reactions belong to which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.explain: In Type II hypersensitivity, IgG or IgM antibodies bind directly to fixed antigens on cell surfaces or extracellular matrix, triggering complement-mediated lysis, opsonization/phagocytosis, or antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).

open.q: Which hypersensitivity type involves IgG or IgM antibodies binding directly to antigens on cell surfaces or basement membranes, as in autoimmune hemolytic anemia?

questions.sub: Active vs Passive Immunity and Hypersensitivity
questions.q: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, systemic lupus erythematosus nephritis, and serum sickness are classic examples of which hypersensitivity mechanism?
options: Type I IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
Type II anti-basement membrane antibody binding
Type III soluble antigen-antibody immune complex deposition
questions.explain: In Type III hypersensitivity, circulating soluble antigen-antibody complexes deposit in small vessel walls, glomeruli, or synovium, activating complement (consuming C3/C4) and attracting neutrophils that release tissue-damaging lysosomal enzymes.

open.q: Which hypersensitivity mechanism underlies serum sickness and acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

questions.q: A 28-year-old man with untreated HIV infection presents with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and oral candidiasis, and his CD4+ T-cell count is 140 cells/uL. Why does selective depletion of CD4+ T helper cells cripple both cell-mediated and humoral immunity?
options: CD4 cells provide cytokines and CD40L signals needed to coordinate macrophages, CD8 cells and B cells
CD4 cells are the only cells that phagocytose fungi in alveoli
CD4 cells directly synthesise serum IgM and IgG
CD4 cells produce complement C3 in the liver
questions.explain: CD4+ helper T cells act as the central orchestrators of adaptive immunity: without their cytokines and CD40L signals, macrophages fail to clear intracellular microbes, CTL responses weaken, and B cells cannot mount T-dependent high-affinity IgG/IgA/IgE responses.

open.q: Why does progressive loss of CD4+ T helper lymphocytes in AIDS impair both humoral and cell-mediated adaptive immunity?
accept: CD4+ T cells provide cytokines and CD40L help needed for B-cell class switching, macrophage activation, and CD8+ T-cell function
Loss of helper T-cell cytokines and costimulation disables B cells, macrophages, and cytotoxic T cells

questions.q: A 7-month-old infant boy presents with recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections after maternal IgG wanes. Labs reveal profoundly reduced IgG, IgA, and IgM and virtually absent circulating B cells, while T-cell counts are normal. Mutation of which enzyme causes X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia?
questions.explain: Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) is required for pre-B-cell receptor signaling; its X-linked mutation arrests B-cell maturation at the pre-B stage in bone marrow, causing absence of plasma cells and all immunoglobulin classes once maternal IgG clears around 6 months.

open.q: Mutation of which signaling enzyme arrests B-cell maturation at the pre-B stage in X-linked agammaglobulinemia?

questions.q: A newborn with cleft palate, congenital heart defects (truncus arteriosus), hypocalcemic tetany, and recurrent viral and fungal infections has an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph due to 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome). Which lymphocyte population is primarily deficient?
questions.explain: Failure of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches to develop results in thymic aplasia/hypoplasia (preventing T-cell maturation) and parathyroid hypoplasia (causing hypocalcemia).

open.q: In DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia due to 22q11.2 deletion), which major lymphocyte population fails to mature?

questions.q: Which anatomical region of a secondary lymph node is the T-cell-dependent zone that becomes markedly expanded during a cell-mediated viral immune response?
questions.explain: In lymph nodes, B cells reside in outer cortical follicles (and germinal centers), plasma cells populate medullary cords, and T lymphocytes occupy the paracortex (which also houses high endothelial venules for lymphocyte entry).

open.q: Name the anatomical zone of a lymph node where T lymphocytes are predominantly localized.

questions.q: Why are asplenic or splenectomized patients particularly susceptible to fulminant sepsis caused by encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningitidis?
options: The spleen clears opsonised encapsulated bacteria and supports IgM responses to capsular polysaccharides
The spleen is the sole site of neutrophil production in adults
Splenectomy removes all CD4 T lymphocytes
The spleen synthesises all serum complement proteins
questions.explain: Splenic marginal zone B cells generate T-independent IgM against bacterial capsular polysaccharides, and splenic red pulp macrophages efficiently filter IgG/C3b-opsonized encapsulated organisms from the bloodstream.

open.q: Why does splenectomy predispose patients to overwhelming infection by encapsulated bacteria?
accept: Loss of splenic macrophage filtration of opsonized bacteria and impaired IgM response to capsular polysaccharides
Decreased clearance of opsonized encapsulated organisms and reduced anti-polysaccharide IgM

questions.q: Which macrophage-derived proinflammatory cytokines act as endogenous pyrogens on the hypothalamus to induce fever and stimulate hepatocytes to synthesize acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein (CRP)?
questions.explain: Activated macrophages release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha: IL-1 and TNF-alpha elevate the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point via PGE2, while IL-6 is the primary driver of hepatic acute-phase protein synthesis (CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A).

open.q: Name the three principal macrophage-derived proinflammatory cytokines that mediate fever and the hepatic acute-phase response.
accept: Interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha

questions.q: In a patient with an acute bacterial infection such as acute appendicitis, a complete blood count shows neutrophilia with a 'left shift'. What does the term 'left shift' signify on a peripheral blood smear?
options: Predominance of hypersegmented neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes
Complete absence of segmented neutrophils in peripheral blood
Increased release of immature neutrophil precursors such as band (stab) forms and metamyelocytes from the bone marrow
questions.explain: Acute infection accelerates marrow granulopoiesis and mobilization of the marrow reserve pool, releasing immature non-segmented band neutrophils and metamyelocytes into peripheral blood ('shift to the left').

open.q: What hematologic finding on a peripheral blood smear is referred to as a 'left shift' during acute bacterial infection?
accept: Increased immature neutrophils such as band forms and metamyelocytes
Elevated band neutrophils in peripheral blood

questions.q: Which portion of an immunoglobulin molecule determines its biological effector functions, such as binding to macrophage Fc receptors, crossing the placenta, or activating complement C1q?
questions.explain: Papain digestion cleaves IgG into two antigen-binding Fab fragments (containing variable regions that bind epitopes) and one crystallizable Fc fragment (composed of heavy chain constant domains that mediate complement fixation and Fc receptor binding).

open.q: Which structural fragment of an antibody molecule mediates effector functions such as complement activation and binding to phagocyte receptors?

questions.q: Which mechanisms generate the vast diversity of antigen-binding receptors on B and T lymphocytes prior to antigen exposure?
options: V(D)J recombination, junctional diversity and random chain pairing generate receptor diversity
Post-translational glycosylation creates all receptor diversity after infection
Millions of complete antibody genes are inherited directly in the germline
Phagocytosis of bacterial plasmids by bone marrow stem cells creates antigen receptors
questions.explain: Random combinatorial joining of Variable (V), Diversity (D), and Joining (J) gene segments by RAG1/RAG2 plus non-templated nucleotide addition by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) generates over 10^11 distinct antigen receptors before antigen encounter.

open.q: Name the DNA recombination process and key enzymes that generate antigen receptor diversity in developing B and T cells before antigen exposure.
accept: V(D)J recombination mediated by RAG1/RAG2 and TdT

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with malar butterfly rash, photosensitive dermatitis, arthritis, proteinuria, and positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies. Serum C3 and C4 levels are markedly depressed. Which mechanism accounts for the low complement levels?
options: Genetic deletion of the C3 gene on chromosome 19
Consumption of classical pathway complement components by widespread circulating immune complexes
Inhibition of hepatic protein synthesis by corticosteroids
Loss of C1q in the feces
questions.explain: In active systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), autoantibodies against nuclear antigens form abundant immune complexes that continuously activate and consume classical pathway proteins (C1, C4, C2, and C3).

open.q: Why are serum C3 and C4 complement levels typically low during an acute flare of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
accept: Consumption of complement by immune complexes via the classical pathway
Classical pathway complement activation and consumption

questions.q: Which lipid mediators are newly synthesized from membrane arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway in mast cells and basophils to cause potent, prolonged bronchoconstriction and vascular leakage during asthma attacks?
questions.explain: Cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4, formerly known as slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis, SRS-A) are generated from arachidonic acid by 5-lipoxygenase and cause sustained airway smooth muscle constriction.

open.q: Name the arachidonic acid metabolites produced by 5-lipoxygenase in mast cells that cause potent, sustained bronchoconstriction in asthma (formerly called SRS-A).

questions.sub: Active vs Passive Immunity and Hypersensitivity
questions.q: How do bacterial superantigens (such as Staphylococcus aureus toxic shock syndrome toxin-1, TSST-1) cause massive cytokine storm and vasodilatory shock?
options: Blocks all MHC class I and II expression on macrophages
Destroys circulating B cells within minutes
Inhibits IL-1 and TNF-alpha release from monocytes
Bridges MHC II and T-cell receptor V-beta regions, activating many T cells and releasing cytokines
questions.explain: Unlike conventional peptide antigens that activate ~0.01% of T cells, superantigens bridge MHC class II and TCR V-beta chains directly without antigen processing, triggering polyclonal activation of ~10-20% of T cells and massive release of IL-2, IFN-gamma, and TNF-alpha.

open.q: Explain how bacterial superantigens like TSST-1 trigger a massive polyclonal T-cell activation and cytokine storm.
accept: Cross-link MHC class II and TCR V-beta chains outside the antigen-binding groove to activate up to 20% of T cells
Bridge MHC class II and TCR V-beta directly without antigen processing
